question.text: In the early years of a closed-ended Category I/II AIF, why is the fund NAV particularly difficult to rely on, per the J-curve discussion?

answer.text: Because management fees compound faster than portfolio growth
Because Indian GAAP prohibits fair-value accounting in early AIF years
Because SEBI requires NAV to be reported at cost in Year 1
Because unrealised investments form a large proportion of total fund value and underlying NAVs may not be representative of eventual cash-flow outcomes

explanation.text: The Logic: Per Section 14.9.1, in early fund stages the unrealised-investment component is high relative to total fund value. Early-stage investee valuations are inherently more uncertain. As the fund matures and realisations happen, NAV converges closer to ultimate gross realisations. This is the NAV-dimension of the classic J-curve. The Trap: Option A fabricates a non-existent cost-reporting rule. Option C is a fee-drag story (separate issue). Option D is factually wrong — IND-AS 113 applies. Cross-Exam Context: XIX-A/B handle J-curve from a client-selling standpoint. XIX-C connects the J-curve to NAV-reliability, which is the LP-reporting angle the manager owns. Manager's Pro-Tip: In LP quarterly letters for Years 1-3, provide TVPI/DPI/RVPI alongside NAV. Sophisticated LPs discount early NAVs and focus on realised proceeds (DPI) and pipeline indicators (mark-ups of follow-on rounds).
